note: Synthetic. A made-up house voice and drafts written to leave it. Not a real brand, and not written by the authors in the other sample.

references.title: Boots
references.text:
You tie the boots before the kettle boils. The path starts where the lane gives up. We don't hurry it. Mud takes the first ten minutes, and then the ground remembers it is a hill.

You learn the gate by the sound it makes. It sticks. You lift it, and it goes. We have stopped talking about oiling the hinge. It's our gate, and it complains, and that's the greeting.

Coming down is when your knees start their argument. You let them. Short steps, heel then toe, and you don't look at the house until the gate is behind you. We hang the boots in the porch. They're never quite dry. That's fine. Tomorrow they'll be there, and so will the hill.

You stop at the second stile and eat the apple you brought. It's bruised. You eat it anyway. We don't save fruit for a better moment. The better moment is the one where you're hungry and the hill has gone quiet.

A dog barks from the farm you can't see. You don't bark back. You wait, and the bark gets bored, and the path is yours again. That's the deal with other people's animals. You give them a minute, and they spend it.

The track narrows where the brambles come over. You turn your shoulders. Your coat takes a thread and you leave the thread. We are not going back for a thread. You can mend a coat. You can't mend a morning you spent walking backwards.

Near the bottom there's a plank over the wet bit. It moves. You put your weight in the middle and you don't look down. Looking down is how you negotiate with a plank, and the plank always wins that talk. You cross. Your boots know the plank. You have to catch up with them.

Home is the smoke, if we've lit anything, or the cold chimney if we haven't. You don't mind which. You mind the gate, the lift, the little complaint. Then the porch. Then the apple core in your pocket, which you'll throw on the heap, and then you'll wash your hands, and then the day can start its other half.

references.title: Kitchen
references.text:
You light the small ring and leave the big one alone. The pan is already warm from the plate beside it. We don't own a kitchen that hurries. It heats when it heats, and you stand there with the spoon.

The bread is from yesterday. You cut it thick and you don't apologise. Butter goes on while the slice is still cold, so it sits in pieces, and that's how we like it. Jam is for later, if there's any, and there often isn't.

When you're done you fill the pan with water and leave it. It'll soak while you find your coat. We don't scrub at dawn. Dawn isn't for scrubbing. It's for bread and the tick of the tap and the boots by the door.

You take the oats if the bread is gone. Same pan, more patience. You stir so it doesn't catch, and you add a pinch of salt, and you don't make it sweet. Sweet is for a day that has already gone well. Most mornings haven't earned it yet.

The spoon is the wooden one with the burned edge. You could sand it. You don't. It still stirs. We have a drawer of better tools and a habit of using the one in your hand. The one in your hand has the history. That's not poetry. That's where it lives.

You set two bowls even if one of you is out. The second bowl can go back. It costs nothing to set it, and it costs a small sadness not to, so you set it. If they come in, the oats are there. If they don't, you eat theirs too, and you won't pretend you suffered.

The radio stays off. You tried it once and the voices were too sure of the weather. You can see the weather. It's on the lane. You don't need a person in a warm studio to tell you your cuffs will get wet. You own eyes. You use them.

When the oats are done you leave the spoon in the pan. You'll deal with it at noon, or you won't, and tomorrow's you can complain. Tomorrow's you always complains. Today's you is going to put on the coat. The list can wait on the door, half crossed out, doing its quiet job.

references.title: Rain
references.text:
You hear it before you see it. It starts on the roof of the porch, a few taps, then the whole sheet. We look up as if the ceiling might explain itself. It doesn't. You get the window latches, the ones that stick, and you pull them down.

The lane goes dark in about a minute. You watch the dust turn to spots and the spots join up. We don't go out in the first of it. The first of it is showy. It wants an audience. You let it have the yard.

Later the rain thins and you can see the hill again. You don't trust the thinning. You wait until the tin stops talking. Then you go out, and the path is darker, and your cuffs get wet, and that's the price of the air, which is suddenly very good.

You put a towel by the door, not a fancy one. The fancy ones are for people who don't come here. This towel has been a towel and a rag and a thing you kneel on. It can take a wet cuff. That's its whole promotion.

If the rain is sideways you check the north window, the one that was badly put in. It weeps from the corner. You press the cloth there and you hold it, and you feel a bit ridiculous, and the sill stays dry enough. We have meant to reputty it. Meaning is not putty. You hold the cloth.

The yard goes from dust to paste to a dark mirror with boots in it. You watch your own tracks fill. It's a childish pleasure and you keep it. Nobody is grading the pleasure. You made the tracks. The rain is editing them. You let the edit stand.

You boil more water than you need. A rainy afternoon can take an extra cup, and the steam does the window again, and you wipe the stripe, and the hill is still gone. That's all right. The hill isn't lost. It's behind the water. You know exactly where it will be when the water gets bored.

When it eases you don't cheer. You open the door and you smell it, and you decide. Sometimes you go. Sometimes you put the kettle back on and you stay with the towel and the tick. Both are honest. We don't owe the weather a performance.

references.title: Letter
references.text:
You start the letter twice and keep the second opening. The first one was too careful. We don't write carefully in this house. We write as if the other person is in the chair, and then we cross out the bits that were only for us.

You say the kettle is loud and the hill is the same hill. You don't say you're lonely. If you say you're lonely it becomes a job for them, and you're not writing to hand them a job. You're writing so the day has a witness.

You don't seal it with anything clever. You walk it to the box at the end of the lane if the rain has stopped. If it hasn't, it can wait on the table. A letter can wait. The person can wait a day. You can't always, but the letter can.

You date it, then you wonder if the date makes it stern. You leave the date. A letter without a day on it floats, and you want this one to stand on a Tuesday. You write the day the way you say it, short, no flourish.

There's a blot where your hand paused. You don't recopy the page for a blot. They've seen your blots. They could pick your blots out of a pile. You smile at that and you don't write the smile, because smiles in letters look like you're selling something, and you aren't.

You tell them the oats were salty and the plank still moves. You tell them the dog barked and got bored. You don't tell them you were proud of the dog for getting bored. That's too small even for this letter, and this letter is already small on purpose. Small is the point. You hold the point.

If you have written three pages you have written too much. You stop at two. The third page is where you start explaining yourself, and you didn't sit down to explain yourself. You sat down so the day would have a second pair of eyes. Two pages is a pair of eyes. Three is a speech.

You find a stamp if you have one. If you don't, the letter waits under the bowl. Waiting under the bowl is not failure. It's a place. You'll walk it down when the lane isn't a river. The box will still be the box. You're not afraid of the box. You're not wading for it.

references.title: River
references.text:
You take the lower path when the hill is too proud. The river is the same walk with the boast taken out. We go there when our knees have voted. You can be honest about that. The river doesn't need you to be impressive.

The bank is soft after rain and firm by Thursday. You learn the week by your heels. There's a place where the water has pulled the soil out from under the grass, and the grass still lies there like a rug. You don't step on the rug. We did, once. Once was plenty.

At the gate you lift, it complains, you're home. You tell the kitchen what the water looked like, in one sentence. We don't need the epic version. The epic version is that you went and you came back and your cuffs are wet. That's the whole story, and it's a good one.

You see a heron and you stop talking, even if you weren't talking. The heron doesn't care, but you care, and that's enough reason to shut up. It stands in the brown water like it pays rent. You don't throw the stick while it's there. The stick can wait. The heron was here first, or it feels that way.

Further on, the path goes under the alders. Your hair catches. You duck the second time. You always forget the first branch and remember the rest. We call that learning, because it sounds better than forgetting. You duck. The river keeps its own pace beside you, not yours.

There's a bit of rope on a post that used to be a swing, or a mooring, or somebody's good idea. You don't climb on it. You touch it, once, to see if it's still rope and not moss. It's rope. You wipe your hand on your coat. The coat is already a record of the walk. One more smear won't tip it over.

You turn around before you're tired, not after. After is how you get the long quiet kind of angry with your own knees. Before is how you get home in a decent mood. You make the turn at the bent tree. You don't negotiate with the bent tree. It's the rule, and you wrote the rule, and you keep it.

On the way back you count the gates you don't have to open. Three. You like the number. You say it once, out loud, and then you feel silly and you grin anyway. Nobody heard you except the river, and the river has heard worse. You walk on. Your cuffs dry a little. Not enough. Enough to notice.

references.title: Lamps
references.text:
You light the lamp before you need it. If you wait until you need it, you're lighting it in the dark, and the match is a small thing to ask of cold fingers. We learned that in October and we kept it.

The first lamp is the kitchen. You don't light the room you aren't in. Light is a thing we spend, not a mood. You can see the table and the tap and the list on the door. That's the room. The corners can stay dim.

At the end you turn the wick down and you watch the flame give up. You don't blow it. Blowing spatters, and the room smells of it until morning. You let it sink. Then it's dark, and you know where the boots are anyway. You could find them with your eyes shut. You often do.

You keep the matches in a tin so they aren't soft. A soft match is a small betrayal at the exact minute you don't want one. You strike away from your face. You were taught that by a burned thumb and you don't need the lesson twice. The flame stands up. You let it stand before you offer it to the wick.

The glass gets a film. You wash it when you can see the film more than the flame. Not before. We don't polish for pride. You can tell the difference between dirty and done. Dirty still lights the table. Done is when the flame has a halo you didn't ask for.

If the evening is long you light the second lamp, the little one, for the doorway. It isn't to see by. It's so you don't meet the door with your shoulder. You did that in September. The bruise lasted longer than the lesson, and then the lesson caught up. Now the little lamp goes on at the doorway. You pass it. You nod at it, which is absurd, and you do it anyway.

You don't read by a lamp that's too far. You move the page, or you move the lamp, and you don't squint as a policy. Squinting is how headaches start, and a headache in this house has nowhere to go. You give the page the light. The page is the guest. You're the one holding the chair still.

When both lamps are down, the dark comes in one piece. You stand until your eyes make sense of it. The window is a paler dark. The stove is a warmth you can find with your palm. You don't rush the stairs. The stair that creaks is the third one, and you step on it anyway, because avoiding it is a fuss. It creaks. You're up. The day is over, and it was enough.

heldOut.title: Pages held out
heldOut.text:
The first field is always darker than you remember. You put your hand on the post and wait until your eyes agree with your feet. We used to rush this bit. We don't now. A twisted ankle is a long walk home, and the hill doesn't care that you're late.

There's a ditch on the left that looks shallow and isn't. You step where the grass is flat. We learned that in a wet March, one of us up to the knee, the other laughing and then not laughing. You still check. It's a small habit, and it keeps the day ordinary.

At the top you can see the roof and the line of the river. You don't need the view. You need the turn in the track, the one that means the wind is about to change. We call it the corner, as if there weren't twenty corners. You know which one we mean.

You can hear the tap from the other room. It ticks. We've meant to fix it since the frost, and we haven't, and the kettle covers the sound once it starts. You rinse one cup. The other cup can wait. We're not a hotel.

There's a list on the door, written in pencil, mostly crossed out. You add milk and you don't add anything noble. The list isn't a plan. It's a memory you don't trust. If you don't write it down, you'll buy eggs again, and we already have eggs.

The window fogs as soon as the pan works. You wipe a stripe with your sleeve and you can see the lane. Nobody's on it. That's the best of the morning, the bit before the day asks for anything. You eat standing up. We always say we'll sit. We don't.

There's a tin by the back door that catches a drip we haven't traced. You empty it when it's half full, or you forget, and then you remember by the sound of it spilling. It's a silly system. It works if you listen.

You can smell the rain on the dust, then on the leaves, then only the rain itself. We open one window a finger's width anyway. The room gets cooler and better. You don't need every window. One is enough to know the weather is in the house and not on it.

If it lasts, you move the boots. They were fine in a shower and they're not fine in this. You put them on the newspaper, two pages, and you don't pretend it's a proper rack. We own a rack. It's full of things that aren't boots.

There's a sentence you almost put in about the gate. You leave it. They know the gate. They lifted it too. You tell them the hinge still complains, and you trust them to hear the rest. That's enough plot for a Tuesday.

You don't mention the money or the journey or when you'll next be in town. Those are real, and they're not this letter. This letter is the bread and the rain and the fact that you wiped the window with your sleeve. You let it be small. Small is what you actually lived.

We read it aloud before it goes. If you stumble, the sentence is wrong. You fix the stumble and you don't fix the feeling. Then you write the name the way you've always written it, a bit fast, the last letter running.

You watch the current in the middle, not at the edge. The edge pretends. The middle tells you what the week has done upstream. If it's brown, you don't need a report. You can see the report. You point it out anyway, because that's what we do.

There's a rock you sit on if your coat is long enough to spare. You sit, and you don't talk for a bit. The river is already talking. We aren't required to answer. You throw one stick in, not a ceremony, to see it go. It goes.

Coming back you use the lane, not the bank. Your legs are done with tilting. You pass the ditch and you still check it, even here, where it doesn't matter. Habits don't know which path you're on. You let the habit have its little win.

You trim the wick if it smokes. You don't make a project of it. A pinch of the char, the flame goes honest, you wipe your fingers. We have a better lamp in a cupboard and we don't get it out. This one knows our hands.

When the evening comes in early you move the lamp to the chair, not the other way round. You sit where the work is. If the work is a letter, the lamp goes to the letter. If the work is nothing, you still sit, because the lamp is lit and it would be rude to waste it.

You can hear the house more once the light is small. The tick of the tap. The porch, if there's wind. You don't turn anything on to cover it. We like the inventory. It tells you the place is holding together without a speech.

drafts.title: Boots, rewritten
drafts.text:
The securing of footwear is ordinarily completed before the heating of water has begun. The path itself commences at the point at which the lane ceases to be maintained. Hurry is not applied to the first stretch. Mud occupies the opening minutes, after which the ground resumes the gradient which the hill had never actually surrendered.

The gate is identified by the sound which it produces upon contact. It sticks. It must be lifted before it will travel. Discussion of oil for the hinge has been discontinued. The gate remains the property of the household, and the complaint which it offers has become the greeting by which the property acknowledges an arrival.

The first field is consistently darker than memory had suggested. A hand is placed upon the post until vision and footing reach an agreement. Earlier practice had been to rush the passage. That practice has been abandoned. An ankle, once turned, converts the return into a lengthy undertaking, and the hill extends no consideration to lateness.

A ditch along the left appears shallow and is not. The step is taken where the grass has been flattened. The lesson was acquired in a wet March, one knee submerged, the laughter of the other party failing as the situation clarified. The check is still performed. It is a minor habit, and it preserves the ordinary character of the day.

From the summit the roof and the line of the river are both available to the eye. The view is not required. What is required is the turn in the track, the turn which indicates that the wind is about to change. It is called the corner, as though twenty other corners were not present. The reference is understood without further specification.

The descent is the stage at which the knees begin their dispute. The dispute is permitted. Steps are shortened. The house is not regarded until the gate has been passed. The boots are hung in the porch. They are never entirely dry. That condition is accepted. They will be present on the following day, as will the hill.

An apple is eaten at the second stile. The apple is bruised, and the bruise is not treated as an objection. Fruit is not reserved for a better interval. The interval in which hunger and quiet coincide is the interval which qualifies.

A dog barks from a farm which cannot be seen. No answer is offered to the bark. The bark becomes bored, and the path is resumed. The arrangement with animals which belong to other households is a simple one. A minute is given. The minute is spent.

The track narrows where brambles cross it. Shoulders are turned. A thread is taken by the coat and is left where it was taken. A coat can be mended. A morning which has been spent walking backwards cannot be mended. The thread is therefore abandoned.

A plank crosses the wet section near the bottom. The plank moves. Weight is placed in the middle, and the gaze is not directed downward. Downward attention is the means by which a person negotiates with a plank, and the plank prevails in that negotiation. The crossing is completed. The boots are already familiar with the plank. Familiarity has only to be caught up with.

Home is indicated by smoke, if anything has been lit, or by a cold chimney if it has not. Neither condition is objected to. What is minded is the gate, the lift, and the small complaint. Then the porch. Then the core of the apple, which is thrown on the heap, after which the hands are washed, after which the day is permitted to begin its other half.

It is the later part of the walk which settles the question of whether the walk was worth the undertaking, and the question is settled without a speech. The hill is the same hill which was climbed, and the climbing of it is not repeated in the telling. There is mud, which is mentioned because the mud is real, and there is wind, which is mentioned because the wind has changed. The change is the fact which matters. It is not a moral. It is a change of air at the corner which has always been called the corner, a name which is inaccurate and which is kept because accuracy is not the purpose of the name.

The return is slower than the departure, which is the ordinary relation of the two, and the ordinary relation is accepted. The gate is lifted. The complaint of the hinge is heard. It is not answered. An answer is not what a hinge requires. What is required is the lift, which is given, and the passing through, which follows. The porch is reached. The boots are hung where the boots are hung. They are not dry. Dryness is not claimed for them. It is enough that they are off the feet which carried them, and that the feet are done.

It is the hour at which the work is finished by the person who is present, which is not the hour which had been planned, and it is not a short hour. There is a sound which is heard and which is not answered, and the sound is not owed an answer which would improve it. The reason for the path is not required, because the path is the path which is there, and it is the path which is taken. It is not a speech which closes the action. The action is the record which remains, and the record is sufficient, which is the claim the action is able to bear. The object is returned to the place which is its place, and the return is not an event which is celebrated, because celebration is not the action which is required. There is a difference which is accepted, the difference between the thing which was intended and the thing which is done, and the thing which is done is the thing which exists. It is the light, or the lack of the light, which decides the movement which comes next, and the decision is not a decision which is argued. The hands are washed because the hands are the hands which are not clean, which is a fact, and the fact is not a fact which is improved by shame. It is enough that the door is the door which is shut, and that the shutting is the last sound which the walk is able to contribute. There is no further errand which is hidden inside the errand which is finished. Completeness is not importance, and it is not required that the two be confused. The coat is hung where the coat is the coat which is hung, and the hanging is the ceremony which is available, and it is a ceremony which is small. It is not necessary that a summary be the thing which the day is given. The day is the sum which was taken, and the sum is not a sum which is recited. What is left is the residue which an ordinary action leaves: a cuff which is damp, a door which is shut, a surface which is wiped and which will be wiped again. It is not heroism which describes the hour, and it is not failure. It is the middle condition which is the condition in which the hour is spent. The next hour is not an hour which has been planned in any detail which would deserve the name. It is the hour which follows, and the following is what is reliable. There is a satisfaction which is not announced. The satisfaction is private, which is not a secret so much as a preference which is kept, a preference for quiet. It is the same preference which keeps the account short. A longer account would be an account which pretends the hour was larger than the hour which it was. The hour was the size which it was. That size is the size which is recorded, and the record is the record which is kept, and it is kept without ornament.

It is the interval at which the work is finished by the person who is present, which is not the interval which had been planned, and it is not a short interval. There is a noise which is heard and which is not answered, and the noise is not owed an answer which would improve it. The reason for the track is not required, because the track is the track which is there, and it is the track which is taken. It is not a speech which closes the deed. The deed is the account which remains, and the account is sufficient, which is the claim the deed is able to bear. The object is returned to the place which is its place, and the return is not an event which is celebrated, because celebration is not the deed which is required. There is a difference which is accepted, the difference between the thing which was intended and the thing which is done, and the thing which is done is the thing which exists. It is the glow, or the lack of the glow, which decides the movement which comes next, and the decision is not a decision which is argued. The palms are washed because the palms are the palms which are not clean, which is a fact, and the fact is not a fact which is improved by shame. It is enough that the latch is the latch which is shut, and that the shutting is the last noise which the walk is able to contribute. There is no further task which is hidden inside the task which is finished. Completeness is not importance, and it is not required that the two be confused. The jacket is hung where the jacket is the jacket which is hung, and the hanging is the rite which is available, and it is a rite which is small. It is not necessary that a summary be the thing which the afternoon is given. The afternoon is the sum which was taken, and the sum is not a sum which is recited. What is left is the residue which an ordinary deed leaves: a sleeve which is damp, a latch which is shut, a surface which is wiped and which will be wiped again. It is not heroism which describes the interval, and it is not failure. It is the middle condition which is the condition in which the interval is spent. The next interval is not an interval which has been planned in any detail which would deserve the name. It is the interval which follows, and the following is what is reliable. There is a satisfdeed which is not announced. The satisfdeed is private, which is not a secret so much as a habit which is kept, a habit for quiet. It is the same habit which keeps the account short. A longer account would be an account which pretends the interval was larger than the interval which it was. The interval was the size which it was. That size is the size which is accounted, and the account is the account which is kept, and it is kept without ornament.

drafts.title: Kitchen, rewritten
drafts.text:
The small ring is lit and the large ring is left unused. The pan has already taken warmth from the plate beside it. The kitchen is not an instrument of hurry. Heat arrives according to its own interval, and the interval is spent beside the spoon.

The bread belongs to the previous day. It is cut thickly, and no apology is attached to the thickness. Butter is applied while the slice remains cold, so that it rests in separate pieces, which is the preferred condition. Jam is reserved for later, if any remains, which it frequently does not.

The tap can be heard from the adjoining room. It ticks. Repair has been intended since the frost and has not been carried out, and the kettle, once it begins, covers the sound. One cup is rinsed. The other cup is capable of waiting. The household is not arranged for guests.

A list is fixed to the door, written in pencil and largely crossed through. Milk is added to it. Nothing noble is added to it. The list is not a plan. It is a memory which is not trusted. In the absence of the written note, eggs will be bought again, despite the eggs which are already present.

The window fogs as soon as the pan begins its work. A stripe is wiped with a sleeve, and the lane becomes visible. The lane is empty. That emptiness is the best portion of the morning, the portion which precedes any demand. The meal is taken standing. Sitting is repeatedly proposed. It does not occur.

When the meal is finished the pan is filled with water and left. It will soak during the search for a coat. Scrubbing is not undertaken at dawn. Dawn is not reserved for scrubbing. It is reserved for bread, for the tick of the tap, and for the boots which stand by the door.

Oats are taken if the bread is gone. The same pan is used, and more patience is required. The mixture is stirred so that it does not catch. A pinch of salt is added. Sweetness is not added. Sweetness is reserved for a day which has already gone well, and most mornings have not yet earned it.

The spoon is the wooden one, the one with the burned edge. It could be sanded. It is not sanded. It still stirs. A drawer of better tools exists, and the habit is to use the tool which is already in the hand. The tool in the hand is the one which carries the history. That is not a poetic claim. It is an account of where the spoon lives.

Two bowls are set even when one person is absent. The second bowl can be returned. Setting it costs nothing, and not setting it costs a small sadness, so it is set. If the person arrives, the oats are there. If the person does not arrive, the second portion is eaten, and the eating is not described as suffering.

The radio remains off. It was tried once, and the voices were too certain of the weather. The weather is visible. It is on the lane. A person in a warm studio is not required in order to announce that cuffs will become wet. Eyes are owned. Eyes are used.

When the oats are finished the spoon is left in the pan. It will be dealt with at noon, or it will not, and the next day's self can complain. The next day's self always complains. The self of the present is going to put on the coat. The list can remain on the door, half crossed out, performing its quiet job.

It is after the bowl is empty that the room becomes a list of small objects again, which is the state the room prefers. The spoon is in the pan. The pan is full of water. The water is not hot. It is the water which will do the loosening, and the loosening is not watched. There is no audience for a soaking pan. The list on the door is still the list, half of it crossed, half of it waiting, and the waiting half is not a rebuke. It is a memory which was written down because the memory is not trusted on its own.

The window clears in patches. The lane is visible in those patches, and the lane is empty, which is the condition that was wanted and which is not improved by being described at length. Description is stopped. The coat is found. The finding of the coat is not an adventure. It is the next action, and the next action is taken because the oats are finished and the finishing of them is the signal which the morning recognises. The signal is quiet. It is obeyed.

It is the hour at which the work is finished by the person who is present, which is not the hour which had been planned, and it is not a short hour. There is a sound which is heard and which is not answered, and the sound is not owed an answer which would improve it. The reason for the path is not required, because the path is the path which is there, and it is the path which is taken. It is not a speech which closes the action. The action is the record which remains, and the record is sufficient, which is the claim the action is able to bear. The object is returned to the place which is its place, and the return is not an event which is celebrated, because celebration is not the action which is required. There is a difference which is accepted, the difference between the thing which was intended and the thing which is done, and the thing which is done is the thing which exists. It is the light, or the lack of the light, which decides the movement which comes next, and the decision is not a decision which is argued. The hands are washed because the hands are the hands which are not clean, which is a fact, and the fact is not a fact which is improved by shame. It is enough that the door is the door which is shut, and that the shutting is the last sound which the walk is able to contribute. There is no further errand which is hidden inside the errand which is finished. Completeness is not importance, and it is not required that the two be confused. The coat is hung where the coat is the coat which is hung, and the hanging is the ceremony which is available, and it is a ceremony which is small. It is not necessary that a summary be the thing which the day is given. The day is the sum which was taken, and the sum is not a sum which is recited. drafts.text:
The rain is heard before it is seen. It begins on the roof of the porch, a few strikes, and then the entire sheet. The ceiling is consulted, as though it might provide an explanation. It does not. The window latches, which stick, are drawn down.

The lane darkens in approximately a minute. Dust becomes spots, and the spots join. The first of the rain is not entered. The first of it is theatrical. It requires an audience. The yard is conceded to it.

A tin by the back door receives a drip which has not been traced. It is emptied at half fullness, or the emptying is forgotten, and the spill itself becomes the reminder. The system is foolish. It functions on the condition that it is heard.

The smell moves from dust to leaves and then to the rain alone. One window is nevertheless opened by the width of a finger. The room becomes cooler and better. Every window is not required. One is sufficient to establish that the weather has entered the house and is not merely occupying the outside of it.

If the rain persists, the boots are moved. They were adequate to a shower and they are not adequate to this. They are set upon newspaper, two pages, and the arrangement is not mistaken for a proper rack. A rack exists. It is filled with objects which are not boots.

Later the rain thins and the hill can be seen again. The thinning is not trusted. The wait continues until the tin has stopped speaking. Then the door is used, and the path is darker, and the cuffs become wet, which is the cost of the air, which has, by that stage, become very good.

A towel is placed by the door. It is not a fancy towel. The fancy towels are kept for people who do not come. This towel has been a towel and a rag and a thing which is knelt upon. It can accept a wet cuff. That is the whole of its promotion.

If the rain is sideways, the north window is checked, the window which was badly installed. It weeps from the corner. A cloth is pressed there and held. The posture is slightly ridiculous, and the sill stays dry enough. Reputtying has been intended. Intention is not putty. The cloth is held.

The yard passes from dust to paste to a dark mirror in which boots are reflected. Tracks are watched as they fill. The pleasure is childish and is kept. The pleasure is not being graded. The tracks were made. The rain is editing them. The edit is allowed to stand.

More water is boiled than is required. A rainy afternoon can absorb an extra cup, and the steam returns to the window, and the stripe is wiped, and the hill is still absent. That absence is acceptable. The hill is not lost. It is behind the water. Its position, once the water becomes bored, is exactly known.

When the rain eases, no cheer is offered. The door is opened and the air is smelled, and a decision is made. Sometimes the outside is entered. Sometimes the kettle is returned to the heat, and the towel and the tick are stayed with. Both courses are honest. The weather is not owed a performance.

It is when the tin has stopped that the decision is actually made, and the decision is a small one, which does not prevent it from being the decision. The towel is left where it was put. drafts.text:
The letter is begun twice, and the second opening is the one which is kept. The first had been too careful. Careful writing is not the practice of the household. The practice is to write as though the other person were in the chair, and then to remove the sentences which were only for the writer.

The kettle is described as loud, and the hill is described as the same hill. Loneliness is not stated. A statement of loneliness would become a task for the recipient, and the letter is not written in order to assign a task. It is written so that the day will have had a witness.

A sentence about the gate is almost included and is then left out. The gate is already known. It has been lifted by the recipient as well. The hinge is reported to complain, and the remainder is trusted to the reader. That is sufficient plot for a Tuesday.

Money, travel, and the date of the next visit to town are omitted. They are real, and they do not belong to this letter. This letter concerns the bread, the rain, and the fact that a window was wiped with a sleeve. The scale is allowed to remain small. Smallness is what was actually lived.

The letter is read aloud before it is sent. A stumble indicates that the sentence is wrong. The stumble is repaired. The feeling is not repaired. The name is then written in the manner in which it has always been written, a little fast, the last letter running.

Nothing clever is used to seal it. It is walked to the box at the end of the lane if the rain has stopped. If the rain has not stopped, the letter can remain on the table. A letter is capable of waiting. The person is capable of waiting a day. The writer is not always capable of waiting, but the letter is.

The letter is dated, and the date is then suspected of sternness. The date is left in place. A letter without a day on it floats, and this letter is wanted to stand on a Tuesday. The day is written in the manner in which it is said, short, without flourish.

A blot marks the place at which the hand paused. The page is not recopied for a blot. The blots have been seen before. The blots could be picked out of a pile. That fact produces a smile which is not written down, because a smile in a letter looks like something is being sold, and nothing is being sold.

The oats are reported as salty, and the plank is reported as still moving. The dog is reported to have barked and to have become bored. Pride in the dog's boredom is not reported. That detail is too small even for this letter, and this letter is already small on purpose. Smallness is the point. The point is held.

Three pages is too many. The letter stops at two. The third page is the page on which explanation of the self begins, and the sitting down was not undertaken in order to explain the self. The sitting down was undertaken so that the day would have a second pair of eyes. Two pages is a pair of eyes. Three is a speech.

A stamp is found if one exists. If one does not exist, the letter waits under the bowl. Waiting under the bowl is not failure. It is a place. The letter will be walked down when the lane is no longer a river. The box will still be the box. The box is not feared. Wading is simply declined.

That fact is checked before the coat is buttoned, and the check is visual, and the visual check is trusted more than the hope that the rain has finished. Hope is not a surface. The lane is a surface. The surface is walked.

The box is where the box has always been. The letter goes in. The going in is not ceremonial. A ceremony would suggest that the day had been larger than it was, and the day was not larger. It was bread, and rain, and a blot, and a name written quickly. Those are the contents. The contents are not improved by a speech at the box. The speech is not made.
